text.p: Nigeria's military government has cancelled an "insensitive" 100 percent increase in domestic air fares annnounced by airlines four days after a plane crashed near Lagos killing all 142 people on board.
"The airfare increase was very insensitive and government had to act swiftly to stop it," said an aviation ministry spokesman on Tuesday.

The airlines, who have long campaigned for an increase in domestic airfares, on Monday began charging double the usual fares but aviation minister Air Commodore Ita Udo-Imeh issued a statement ordering them to revert to old fares immediately.
"The increase is illegal, unauthorised as well as an act of economic sabotage against the people and government of the federal republic of Nigeria," his statement said.
The airlines immediately complied and resumed charging the former fares, which they consider not enough to sustain their operations in an economy that has been in recession for years.
An economy one-way ticket to the capital Abuja from Lagos, a distance of about 800 km, (500 miles) costs 2,650 ($33.12).
Airline operators say this needs to rise by 170 percent for them to make any profit.

"An increase would not only assist in putting our aircraft in good and air worthy conditions but importation of spare parts will become feasible," said the chief executive of one of many wholly Nigerian-owned airlines that operate domestic flights.

The cause of last Thursday's crash of ADC airline's Boeing 727 coming from the southeastern city of Port Harcourt has not yet been established but avaition experts are already blaming such accidents on the tight squeeze in the industry.

"It is obvious that the airlines are mainly surviving by sheer dint of doggedness," said aviation correspondent Amanze Obi of the independent Thisday newspaper, adding "A lot of things are compromised. The aircraft are hardly maintained."

Thisday dubs many aircraft operated in Nigeria "flying coffins" on account of lack of maintenance and the fact that many are from former communist countries with manuals in languages foreign to Nigerian pilots.
The aviation ministry spokesman said the government was aware of the problems faced by the airline industry but any local fare increase had to be approved by the utilities board.
